title: Not reconciling
hookLine: forgiving doesn't require going back to the relationship

cards: Two brothers meet on a road. Jacob, the younger, once tricked Esau out of their father's blessing and ran for his life. Now he is coming home, bracing for the worst.

And Genesis says: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." A few weeks back, this path stood with Esau as he ran. Today, read on to the end of the chapter.
The chapter keeps going. Esau offers to travel on together. Jacob gently says no.
And the two brothers take two different roads.

teach.b: The psychology of forgiveness draws a line here. Everett Worthington, whose five steps came two days ago, titled one of his books Forgiving and Reconciling, and he treats them as two different things.
Forgiving can happen inside one person. Reconciling takes two, and it needs trust to be rebuilt, which takes behavior over time from both sides. You can do the first alone, not the second.
After the embrace, Jacob says his children are young and his flocks are slow, and he'll follow at their pace. Esau goes home to Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth.
The text doesn't tell us why Jacob holds back. Some readers hear caution; some hear wisdom; some hear a man who still can't quite believe he's forgiven.
What the story does show is an embrace that is real and a distance that stays.

An older pair in the same book: when the herdsmen of Abram, as Abraham is still called there, keep quarreling with his nephew Lot's herdsmen, Abram says: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee."
And his answer to keeping the peace is space: "separate thyself, I pray thee, from me." Peace, kept by distance. Some relationships can be rebuilt, and that can be good.

teach.h: NO ONE HAS TO WALK BACK INTO HARM.
teach.b: Others shouldn't be, because going back would mean walking into the same harm. Forgiveness, as Worthington describes it, doesn't ask anyone to walk back in.
It can be done from across a field.

how: Some counselors who work with forgiveness separate it from reconciliation: a person may forgive privately, in writing that is never sent or in prayer, without restoring contact.

o: making peace by pretending the harm never happened
refusing to forgive until the other person apologizes
forgiving someone without letting them back into your life

s: in Worthington's view, forgiving someone means you must let them back into your life

games.q: you're Jacob. your brother has just embraced you and forgiven you, and now he offers to travel on together. what does the text say you do?
o: travel on with him, side by side.
decline gently and go a different way.
refuse to speak to him at all.
games.why: Jacob says his children and flocks are slow and he'll follow at their pace. Esau goes home to Seir; Jacob goes to Succoth. the embrace was real, and so is the distance.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're no longer close to, or don't want to be close to again, and leave them where they are, small and far away across a wide field.

From where you sit, let the rope between you go slack: you're not walking over or calling them, only letting go of your end. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer from right where you are; the gap stays.

wordCard.voice: Not reconciling. Forgiving can happen inside one person; reconciling takes two and rebuilt trust. You can forgive and still keep the distance. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: from a distance. The embrace was real, and so was the road apart. Day nine hundred sixty-nine, done.
